Let $q$ be any formal polynomial of degree at most $n$ with $q(x_i)=y_i$. Extend the actual coefficient lists of $p$ and $q$ by zeros through index $n$, obtaining vectors $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$; these are vectors for their evaluations, not padded formal objects. The vector $c_k=a_k-b_k$ defines by [F3] a formal polynomial $r$ of degree at most $n$; [F5] gives $r(t)=p(t)-q(t)$ for every real $t$. Since $p$ and $q$ agree at all nodes by step 1.1 and the choice of $q$, $r$ has the $n+1$ distinct roots $x_0,\ldots,x_n$. If $r$ were nonzero, [F4] would give at most $\deg r\le n$ roots, a contradiction. Hence $r$ is the zero formal polynomial; by [F3], every $a_k-b_k=0$. The canonical coefficient lists of $p$ and $q$ are therefore identical, so $p=q$.
This proves that the interpolant from step 1.1 is the unique formal polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying the node values.

Suppose $x$ is not a node. By [F8], $\omega_n(x)\ne0$, so set $c=(f(x)-p(x))/\omega_n(x)$ and define $g(t)=f(t)-p(t)-c\omega_n(t)$ on $[a,b]$. At every node $x_j$, [F2] gives $f(x_j)=p(x_j)$ and [F1] gives $\omega_n(x_j)=0$, so $g(x_j)=0$; by the choice of $c$, also $g(x)=0$.

By [F8], $\omega_n$ is monic of degree $n+1$ and $p$ has degree at most $n$, so their coefficients at degree $n+1$ are respectively $1$ and $0$. Applying [F5] to these two polynomials gives $p^{(n+1)}(\xi)=0$ and $\omega_n^{(n+1)}(\xi)=(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}$.

Sort the $n+2$ distinct points consisting of the nodes and $x$ as $z_0<\cdots<z_{n+1}$. The function $f$ is $C^{n+1}$ by [F3]; $p$ has degree at most $n$ and $\omega_n$ has degree $n+1$ by [F8]. Their iterated derivatives through order $n+1$ exist by [F5]. Repeated application of the sum and scalar-multiple rules [F6] shows that $g$ is $(n+1)$-times differentiable on $(z_0,z_{n+1})$. Also, $f$ is continuous by [F3], the polynomial functions $p$ and $\omega_n$ are continuous by [F7], and the finite linear combination defining $g$ is continuous on $[z_0,z_{n+1}]$ by [F7]. Apply [F4] with $m=n+1$ to the zeros from step 1.2. This yields $\xi\in(z_0,z_{n+1})$ with $g^{(n+1)}(\xi)=0$.

Differentiate the defining identity for $g$ $n+1$ times at $\xi$. Step 2.1 licenses these derivatives and [F6] preserves the linear combination, so $0=g^{(n+1)}(\xi)=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)-c(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}$. By [F9] the factorial factor is nonzero, so $c=f^{(n+1)}(\xi)/(n+1)!_{\mathbb R}$.
Substituting the value of $c$ into its definition in step 1.2 gives the claimed remainder formula. Since $z_0=\min\{x,x_0\}$ and $z_{n+1}=\max\{x,x_n\}$, $\xi$ lies in the stated interval.

Weight construction visits at most $(n+1)n$ node pairs and performs finitely many checked operations. Each operation either returns a value in $\mathbb F$ or returns *range_failure*, which stops the procedure, so this stage terminates.

If weight construction completes, the evaluation loop visits exactly $n+1$ terms. Every checked operation either returns a value in $\mathbb F$ or exits with *range_failure*. After the loop, a zero denominator returns *range_failure*; otherwise the checked final division either returns *range_failure* or returns *success* with a value in $\mathbb F$.
These cases exhaust the procedure's branches and every loop is finite, so every input terminates with a declared status.
